cohort: The participants were 412 infants representative of U.S. demographic diversity.
finding: A widespread Bifidobacterium deficit was observed in approximately 25% of U.S. infants, which was associated with distinct microbiome features (reduced antimicrobial resistance/virulence factors, altered carbohydrate utilization/metabolic signatures) and suggested to contribute to the development of atopy.
mod_finding: In C-section birth infants, Bifidobacterium tended to be replaced by potentially pathogenic species in the human milk oligosaccharide utilization niche.
